ts:0.prompt: Two interfaces with the same name are declared in one file. What happens?
options: The second declaration is a compile error (duplicate identifier)
The two declarations are merged into one interface with all members
The last declaration silently replaces the first one
Only the first declaration is kept and the other is ignored
ts:0.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging: members from every declaration are combined. A type alias declared twice is a duplicate identifier error. Merging is how libraries let you augment global types such as Window or Express.Request.

ts:0.prompt: What is the type of x['a'] here?
ts:0.explanation: An intersection of object types intersects each property too, and string & number has no possible values, so the property becomes never. Such a type is effectively impossible to construct.
ts:0.code:
type A = { a: string } & { a: number };
declare const x: A;

ts:0.prompt: An interface extends another but redeclares a property with an incompatible type. What happens compared with using an intersection?
options: Both silently produce a union of the two property types
extends reports an error at the declaration, an intersection quietly gives never
extends gives never, an intersection reports an error at the declaration
Neither complains because TypeScript is structurally typed
ts:0.explanation: interface extends checks that the redeclared property is assignable to the base's, and errors if not. & just combines the types, so conflicting properties silently collapse to never and the problem only shows up when you try to build a value.

ts:0.prompt: Why does this fail to compile?
options: toFixed does not exist on every member of the union string | number
The parameter must be annotated with a generic to access methods
toFixed was removed from the number type in strict mode
Union types never allow any method calls
ts:0.explanation: On a union you can only use members that exist on all constituents. Narrow first with typeof x === 'number', then call toFixed.

ts:0.prompt: Which of these is a compile error?
options: const o = { name: 'a', age: 1 }; const p: { name: string } = o;
const p: { name: string } = { name: 'a', age: 1 };
const p = { name: 'a' } as { name: string };
ts:0.explanation: Excess property checking only applies to fresh object literals assigned directly to a typed target. Going through a variable (first option) is allowed because the shape is still compatible.

ts:0.prompt: Which construct can only be written with a type alias, not an interface?
options: A union such as type ID = string | number
An object shape with optional members
A shape that a class implements
A shape that extends another shape
ts:0.explanation: Interfaces describe object shapes (and callable shapes). Unions, primitives, tuples and mapped or conditional types need type aliases. For plain object shapes the two are mostly interchangeable.

ts:1.prompt: Inside the if block, what is the type of x?
ts:1.explanation: typeof null is 'object', so typeof x === 'object' keeps null in the union. TypeScript doesn't remove it, so check x !== null as well.

ts:1.prompt: How does the in operator narrow a union?
options: It narrows to the members that have (or may have) the property in the true branch
It only works on class instances
It narrows by checking the property's value type, not its presence
It never narrows; it is runtime only
ts:1.explanation: 'swim' in pet narrows Fish | Bird to the members that declare swim in the true branch and to the rest in the false branch. It's a lightweight way to discriminate shapes without a tag field.

ts:1.prompt: A new member is added to the union Shape. What happens to this function?
options: It fails to compile because s in default is no longer never
It compiles and returns undefined for the new member
The new member is automatically handled by the default branch
It throws at runtime only if called with the new member and nothing is reported at compile time
ts:1.explanation: Assigning s to a never-typed variable in the default branch is the exhaustiveness check. If a case is missing, s is the unhandled member, which isn't assignable to never, so the compiler points to the function.

ts:1.prompt: What does the predicate return type x is string actually guarantee?
options: Nothing beyond what you implement, TypeScript trusts the function
The compiler checks the body really tests for string
The function is inlined at compile time
The parameter is converted to string at runtime
ts:1.explanation: A user-defined type guard is an assertion the compiler takes on faith. If the body returns true for a non-string, the narrowing is wrong and the type system can't tell.

ts:1.prompt: What is the type of x inside the if block?
ts:1.explanation: Both undefined and the empty string '' are falsy, so in the falsy branch TypeScript can't rule out string. Narrowing by truthiness is lossy for strings and numbers; compare with === undefined when that is what you mean.

ts:1.prompt: What does an assertion function with the signature asserts x is string do after a call?
options: Narrows x to string for the code after the call if the call returns normally
Converts x to string at runtime
Returns a boolean the caller must check
ts:1.explanation: Assertion functions throw when the condition fails, so the code after them can rely on the narrowing. Node's assert and zod-based helpers use this form.

options: Static members belong to the class, not an instance, so they cannot use the instance type parameter T
Static properties can only be of primitive types
T is only available inside constructors
Generic classes cannot have static members at all
ts:2.explanation: Type parameters belong to instances (Box<number> vs Box<string>), but there is only one static side per class. A static method can declare its own type parameter instead.

ts:2.prompt: What is the return type of first([]) under strict mode?
ts:2.explanation: An empty array literal is inferred as never[] with strictNullChecks, so T is never and the call's return type is never. Pass the type explicitly, first<number>([]), when you need something else.

ts:2.prompt: In a .tsx file, which generic arrow function declaration parses correctly?
ts:2.explanation: In TSX, <T> looks like a JSX element. A trailing comma (<T,>) or <T extends unknown> disambiguates it. Declarations with the function keyword don't have the problem.

ts:2.prompt: What is the type of R?
ts:2.explanation: A conditional type on a naked type parameter distributes over a union: string gives 'y' and number gives 'n', so the result is the union. Wrap the parameter in a tuple ([T] extends [string]) to stop distribution.
ts:2.code:
type IsString<T> = T extends string ? 'y' : 'n';
type R = IsString<string | number>;

ts:2.explanation: infer declares a type variable inside the extends clause of a conditional type. Matching number[] against (infer U)[] binds U to number. It is how ReturnType and Awaited are written.
ts:2.code: type ElementType<T> = T extends (infer U)[] ? U : never;

ts:2.prompt: What is the type of r?
ts:2.explanation: A type parameter constrained to a primitive like string is inferred as the literal type 'a'. Unconstrained T would give string for a mutable binding, but literal inference is kept when the constraint includes primitives.
ts:2.code:
function f<T extends string>(x: T): T { return x; }
const r = f('a');

ts:3.prompt: Omit<User, 'nme'> is a compile error because 'nme' is not a key of User.
ts:3.explanation: Omit's key parameter is K extends keyof any, so typos are accepted and nothing is omitted. Pick requires real keys. Write your own StrictOmit with K extends keyof T if you want the check.

ts:3.prompt: A Partial<Config> has a nested object property. What about that property's own fields?
options: They stay required because Partial is shallow
ts:3.explanation: Partial, Required and Readonly only map the top-level properties. For deep versions you need a recursive mapped type (DeepPartial) or a library.
ReturnType of an async function is Promise<User>. Awaited unwraps promises (recursively), giving User.

options: An object with both keys a and b of type number
An object with at least one of the keys
ts:3.explanation: Record<K, V> with a union of literals maps each member to V, and all of them are required. Use Partial<Record<...>> if some may be absent.
Extract keeps the union members assignable to the second argument, Exclude removes them. Exclude<'a'|'b'|'c','a'|'c'> would be 'b'.

options: An object type { to: string; body?: string }
ts:3.explanation: Parameters<F> gives the argument list as a (labelled) tuple type. It is handy for wrappers that forward arguments.
ts:3.code: declare function send(to: string, body?: string): void;

ts:3.prompt: Readonly<T> makes the object immutable at runtime like Object.freeze does.
ts:3.explanation: Readonly is a compile-time check that erases to nothing. Use Object.freeze (shallow) for runtime protection.

ts:4.prompt: Why does this fail to compile?
options: unknown must be narrowed before it is assigned to a more specific type
unknown cannot be declared with const
string is not assignable from any value type
Variables cannot be reassigned between types
ts:4.explanation: unknown is the type-safe top type: anything can be assigned to it, but you can't use it or assign it elsewhere until you narrow with typeof, instanceof or a guard.
ts:4.code:
const v: unknown = 'hi';
const s: string = v;

ts:4.prompt: What does a function that always throws return best typed as?
ts:4.explanation: never means the function never returns normally. void means it returns but the result is meaningless. The distinction lets control flow analysis treat code after the call as unreachable.

ts:4.prompt: What is the effect of any on the following line?
options: It compiles; any switches off checking for the whole property chain
It is a compile error because foo is not known
It narrows x to the object type
ts:4.explanation: Every property access, call and index on any is allowed and yields any, so errors move to runtime. That's why unknown is preferred for untrusted values.
ts:4.code:
const x: any = 1;
const y = x.foo.bar.baz;

ts:4.prompt: What is the type of e in the catch block with strict mode on (TS 4.4+)?
ts:4.explanation: useUnknownInCatchVariables, enabled by strict, makes catch variables unknown. Narrow with e instanceof Error before reading message.

ts:4.prompt: What does type T = string | never reduce to?
ts:4.explanation: never is the empty set, the identity for unions, so any union with it simplifies away. Conversely string & never is never, and any | string is any.

ts:4.prompt: JSON.parse returns any. What is the safest way to consume its result?
options: Assign to unknown and validate it, for example with a zod schema
Cast with as to the target interface
Declare the target variable as any
Wrap it in a type guard that always returns true
ts:4.explanation: A cast doesn't check anything, so bad data flows through typed code. Validating the unknown value gives a real guarantee that the shape matches.

options: A function returning a value is assignable to one returning void, the caller just ignores the result
TypeScript treats void as an alias for any
Arrow functions are exempt from return checks
It is not legal and will error
ts:4.explanation: Contextual return type void means 'caller won't use the result', which is why arr.forEach(x => list.push(x)) compiles. The rule only applies to function types, not to declared function bodies.

ts:5.prompt: What does E[0] give at runtime?
ts:5.explanation: Numeric enums compile to an object with a reverse mapping, so both E.A === 0 and E[0] === 'A'. String enums don't have the reverse mapping.

ts:5.prompt: Why does this fail to compile?
options: String enum members are opaque, a raw string literal is not assignable to the enum type
ts:5.explanation: String enums are nominal-ish: only Dir.Up is assignable to Dir, not the equal string. That avoids accidental mixing but makes serialisation boundaries need explicit conversion.
ts:5.code:
enum Dir { Up = 'UP' }
const d: Dir = 'UP';

ts:5.prompt: How do you derive the union 'GET' | 'POST' from this object?
ts:5.explanation: as const keeps literal values, typeof gets the object type, and indexing by keyof gives the union of its values. keyof alone would give the keys ('get' | 'post').
ts:5.code: const Methods = { get: 'GET', post: 'POST' } as const;

ts:5.prompt: What is the type of arr?
ts:5.explanation: as const makes the array a readonly tuple of literal types. That's why it can safely be mapped into union types.

ts:5.prompt: What does satisfies change compared with a type annotation?
options: It checks the shape but keeps the inferred, narrower type of the value
It checks the shape at runtime
It widens the value to the annotation type
ts:5.explanation: With const p: Record<string, number> = {a: 1}, p.b is allowed and typed number. With satisfies, p keeps the exact keys, so p.b errors, while a wrong value type is still caught.
ts:5.code: const p = { a: 1 } satisfies Record<string, number>;

ts:5.prompt: Enums emit JavaScript code, whereas interfaces and type aliases are erased.
ts:5.explanation: enum compiles to an object (IIFE). Because of that, runtimes that only strip types (Node's type stripping, erasableSyntaxOnly in TS 5.8) don't support them; a const object plus a union type is the erasable alternative.

ts:6.prompt: Which flag is NOT turned on by strict: true?
ts:6.explanation: strict covers strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny, noImplicitThis, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, strictPropertyInitialization, alwaysStrict and useUnknownInCatchVariables. noUncheckedIndexedAccess is opt-in on top.

ts:6.prompt: With noUncheckedIndexedAccess enabled, what is the type of arr[0] for arr: number[]?
ts:6.explanation: Index signatures and array indexing can return undefined at runtime, and this flag makes that explicit. You then handle undefined or use non-null assertions deliberately.

ts:6.prompt: With moduleResolution nodenext, how must a relative import of ./util.ts be written in source?
ts:6.explanation: Node's ESM resolution requires explicit file extensions, and TypeScript expects you to write the emitted .js extension. (allowImportingTsExtensions is the exception for noEmit setups.)

ts:6.prompt: What does the isolatedModules flag force you to do when re-exporting a type?
options: Use export type so single-file transpilers can erase it
ts:6.explanation: Transpilers like esbuild and SWC compile each file alone and can't know whether a re-exported name is a type. export type { Foo } makes it explicit.

ts:6.prompt: What is the difference between target and lib?
options: target sets the emitted JS syntax level, lib sets which built-in type declarations are available
target sets typings, lib sets output syntax
ts:6.explanation: target ES2017 decides whether async or classes are down-levelled; lib decides if Promise.allSettled or Array.prototype.at exist in the types. You may need to bump lib without changing target.

options: Type checking of your own .ts files
ts:6.explanation: It speeds up builds and avoids conflicts between dependencies' typings, at the cost of not detecting errors inside them.

options: Compile error: an async function's return type must be Promise<T>
ts:7.explanation: An async function always returns a promise, so the annotation has to be Promise<number>. The body still returns a plain number.

ts:7.prompt: What is the type of result?
ts:7.explanation: Promise.all keeps a tuple type, with each position awaited. Using the tuple preserves distinct types, so there's no need for casts.
Awaited unwraps nested promise (thenable) types recursively, mirroring what await does at runtime.

ts:7.prompt: Does the TypeScript type system track which errors a function may throw?
options: No, thrown errors are not part of function types
ts:7.explanation: There is no checked-exceptions concept. Model expected failures as values, for example a Result<T, E> discriminated union, and treat catch variables as unknown.

ts:7.prompt: What is the main benefit of a Result<T, E> discriminated union over throwing?
options: Callers are forced by the compiler to handle the failure branch
It runs faster than exceptions in all engines
It removes the need for async code
ts:7.explanation: { ok: true, value } | { ok: false, error } requires narrowing on ok before the value can be used, so ignoring an error becomes a type error.

ts:7.prompt: Why is an async callback passed to forEach a common bug the type checker allows?
options: forEach expects a void-returning callback, so the returned promise is ignored and not awaited
Async functions cannot be arrow functions
ts:7.explanation: The return type void accepts a function returning Promise<void>, so the compiler is satisfied but the loop doesn't wait. Use for...of with await or Promise.all(map(...)); the no-misused-promises lint rule flags it.

ts:8.prompt: What does z.infer<typeof UserSchema> give you?
options: The static TypeScript type matching the schema's output
ts:8.explanation: It derives the TS type from the schema, so the validator and the type can't drift apart. There is one source of truth.

ts:8.prompt: What is the difference between parse and safeParse?
options: parse throws a ZodError on failure, safeParse returns a result object with success true or false
parse is async, safeParse is sync
safeParse mutates the input, parse does not
ts:8.explanation: Use safeParse in request handlers to build a 400 response without try/catch, parse where invalid data is a bug.

ts:8.prompt: Because the TypeScript type says a field is a number, the server can trust request bodies without validation.
ts:8.explanation: Types are erased at runtime and an incoming HTTP body is just unknown data. Validate at the boundary (zod) and let the validated value flow in as typed.

ts:8.prompt: By default, what does z.object do with unknown keys in the input?
ts:8.explanation: The default is strip. Use .strict() to reject unknown keys, which is useful to catch typos in config, or a loose object to keep them.

ts:8.prompt: What does z.coerce.number() do with the input '42'?
options: Converts it to the number 42 before validating
Rejects it because it is a string
ts:8.explanation: Coercion runs Number(input) first, which is handy for query strings and form data that arrive as text. Beware that null and '' coerce to 0.

ts:8.prompt: What is the difference between .optional() and .nullable()?
options: optional allows undefined, nullable allows null
optional allows null, nullable allows undefined
ts:8.explanation: nullish() allows both. JSON APIs often send null for 'empty' while JS destructuring defaults only kick in for undefined, so the distinction matters.
